package_info.package_manager: N/A (delivered via phishing, not a public package repository)
package_info.why_malicious: MrAnon Stealer is a multi-stage info-stealer malware distributed via phishing emails. It leverages a combination of .NET, PowerShell, and Python (cx-Freeze packed) payloads to steal credentials, browser sessions, cryptocurrency wallets, and sensitive files. The malware exfiltrates stolen data to public file-sharing sites and the attacker's Telegram channel, using deceptive techniques to evade user suspicion and security controls.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Downloader link hidden in PDF stream object, which, when clicked, downloads a .NET executable (adobe.exe) from anonbin[.]ir.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When the user opens the PDF and clicks the hidden downloader link, the PDF initiates a network request to download a .NET executable from anonbin[.]ir, resulting in the delivery of the next-stage malware payload.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Embedding hidden downloader links in PDFs is a well-known phishing tactic to deliver malware, especially when the link points to an untrusted domain and downloads an executable.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate PDFs should not contain hidden links that trigger the download of executable files from suspicious or untrusted domains.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Corporate or informational PDFs may contain visible hyperlinks, but these should not initiate downloads of executables from unknown sources.
key_indicators: Downloader link hidden in PDF stream object

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: The .NET executable uses ScriptRunner.dll to extract Scripts.zip, then unpacks and executes down2.ps1 via PowerShell.exe.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Upon execution of the downloaded .NET executable, the code unpacks an embedded PowerShell script from Scripts.zip using ScriptRunner.dll, writes it to disk, and launches it via PowerShell.exe, enabling the next stage of the attack.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Dropping and executing PowerShell scripts from within a .NET executable is a common malware technique to evade detection and escalate the attack chain.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate installers or applications do not silently unpack and execute PowerShell scripts from embedded resources without user consent or transparency.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some enterprise deployment tools may use embedded scripts, but these are typically signed, well-documented, and do not execute without user awareness.
key_indicators: Automatic extraction and execution of script
Use of ScriptRunner.dll to unpack Scripts.zip

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: PowerShell script loads a Windows Form, fetches a zip payload from anonbin[.]ir, decompresses it, and executes python.exe. Displays a fake error window ('File Not Supported', 'Not Run: python.exe') to mislead the user.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When the PowerShell script is executed, it loads a Windows Form to interact with the user, downloads a zip archive from anonbin[.]ir, extracts python.exe from the archive, executes the binary, and displays a fake error message to mislead the user into thinking the payload did not run.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Downloading and executing binaries from the internet via PowerShell, combined with user deception through fake error dialogs, is a hallmark of multi-stage malware delivery.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate PowerShell scripts should not fetch and execute remote binaries or attempt to deceive users with misleading error messages.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some IT automation scripts may download and run trusted tools, but these actions are typically logged, transparent, and do not use deception.
key_indicators: Display of fake error message to mask execution

execution_context.file_location: python.exe (from extracted zip, not a legitimate Python interpreter)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: python.exe (cx-Freeze packed) searches for \lib\library.zip and loads cstgversion__main__.pyc using PyObject_CallObject.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Upon execution of the dropped python.exe, the binary searches for the bundled library.zip archive, loads the cstgversion__main__.pyc module using PyObject_CallObject, and initiates the malicious info-stealer logic.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Non-standard Python executables that load obfuscated code from bundled archives are a common method for malware to evade static analysis and detection.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate Python applications do not typically obfuscate their main logic in compiled .pyc files within a zip archive, nor do they use custom loaders in this manner.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some commercial software may use cx-Freeze for packaging, but the main logic is not hidden in this way and is usually signed and verifiable.
key_indicators: Loads .pyc file from library.zip using PyObject_CallObject
Non-standard python.exe not matching official Python distribution

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Malware terminates processes (e.g., ArmoryQt.exe, chrome.exe, Discord.exe, etc.), captures screenshot, collects browser data, wallet data, files with sensitive extensions, compresses data, uploads to gofile[.]io, and sends download link/system info to Telegram via bot token.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When the malicious Python code is executed, it terminates selected processes (such as browsers, cryptocurrency wallets, and Discord), captures a screenshot, collects browser credentials, wallet data, and files with sensitive extensions, compresses the stolen data, uploads it to gofile[.]io, and sends the download link and system information to the attacker's Telegram bot.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The combination of process termination, mass data theft, screenshot capture, and exfiltration to both public file-sharing sites and Telegram is characteristic of advanced info-stealer malware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not kill unrelated processes, harvest sensitive data, or exfiltrate it to unknown servers or messaging platforms.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Backup or diagnostic tools may collect some system data, but never terminate unrelated processes or exfiltrate data to public or attacker-controlled channels.
key_indicators: Process termination of browsers, wallets, and security tools
Bulk data compression and upload to gofile[.]io
Notification to attacker's Telegram bot with exfiltrated data link

attack_chain.action: User receives phishing email with malicious PDF attachment.
attack_chain.leads_to: User opens PDF and clicks downloader link.

attack_chain.action: Downloader link in PDF fetches .NET executable (adobe.exe) from remote server.
.NET executable unpacks and runs PowerShell script (down2.ps1).
PowerShell script downloads and extracts zip payload, executes python.exe, and displays fake error message.
python.exe loads and executes malicious Python code from library.zip.
Malicious Python code steals data, exfiltrates to gofile[.]io, and sends notification to attacker's Telegram.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker receives stolen data and system info.

behavioral_signatures: PDF attachments with hidden downloader links that initiate executable downloads
Execution of .NET binaries that unpack and run embedded PowerShell scripts
PowerShell scripts that download and execute remote binaries and display fake error dialogs
Presence of cx-Freeze packed Python executables loading .pyc files from library.zip
Process termination of browsers, cryptocurrency wallets, and security tools
Bulk collection and compression of files with sensitive extensions
Exfiltration of data to public file-sharing sites (e.g., gofile[.]io)
Outbound connections to Telegram API using hardcoded bot tokens
file_indicators: adobe.exe in %TEMP% or user download directory
python.exe (non-standard, not matching official Python interpreter)
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for emails with PDF attachments containing hidden downloader links that initiate executable downloads. Detect execution of .NET binaries that unpack and run embedded PowerShell scripts, especially those that download further payloads from suspicious domains. Flag PowerShell scripts that download and execute binaries, display fake error dialogs, or drop non-standard python.exe files. Look for cx-Freeze packed Python executables loading .pyc files from library.zip. Alert on process termination of browsers, wallets, and security tools, as well as bulk file compression and uploads to public file-sharing sites or Telegram bots. Correlate network activity to known malicious domains and Telegram API usage with suspicious bot tokens.
